questions.question: What was the reported ordering of nanoparticle toxicity across the six materials?

options.A: Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2.
options.B: CuO > Ag > Au > ZnO > SiO2 > TiO2.
options.C: Ag > ZnO > CuO > TiO2 > Au > SiO2.
options.D: SiO2 > TiO2 > Au > ZnO > CuO > Ag.

questions.rationale: The abstract explicitly ranks silver as most toxic and silica as least toxic in the tested panel.
questions.evidence_quote: The toxicity of the nanoparticles was compared and the order of toxicity is estimated as Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2.

questions.question: What were the baseline control hatching rate and viability of hatched nauplii?
questions.rationale: The control baseline was substantially higher than the rates under the most toxic nanoparticle exposures.
questions.evidence_quote: Brine shrimp normally showed a hatching rate of 74%+5.5, the viability of these hatched nauplii was about 97%.

questions.question: At 100 mg/L, what hatching outcome was reported for Ag and CuO nanoparticles?

options.A: Hatching fell to about 29%, and only about half of hatched nauplii were motile/viable.
options.C: Hatching fell to 10%, but all hatchlings remained motile.

questions.rationale: Silver and copper oxide produced the strongest hatching effects; viability among hatchlings was also reduced at the high concentration.
questions.evidence_quote: The highest effect was seen in presence of silver and copper oxide nanoparticles. The hatching rate dropped to about 29% in the two nanoparticles; of these only 50% were motile and viable at a concentration of 100mg/L

questions.question: What was the 24-hour LC50 reported for silver nanoparticles in the larval assay?
questions.rationale: The article reports a 24-hour LC50 near 10.12 mg/L for silver nanoparticles.
questions.evidence_quote: The nauplii showed variability in viability to various nanoparticles. The most toxic was the silver nanoparticles and silver in ionic form (Table 2 ). Silver in ionic form was highly toxic as 80% of the nauplii were dead in 24 hours in silver nitrate solution (Figure 4 ). The LC 50 of the silver nanoparticles was around 10.12mg/L at 24hours.

questions.question: How did the silver nitrate result compare with nanoparticle exposure at 24 h?

options.A: Silver nitrate killed 80% of nauplii within 24 h, indicating strong toxicity of ionic silver as well.
options.B: Silver nitrate caused no mortality, showing only particles were toxic.
options.C: Silver nitrate killed 8% of nauplii, less than controls.

questions.rationale: The soluble ionic form was itself highly toxic, so the authors did not attribute all observed silver effects solely to nanoparticle form.
questions.evidence_quote: Silver in ionic form was highly toxic as 80% of the nauplii were dead in 24 hours in silver nitrate solution

questions.question: What was the reported correlation between hatching-rate effects and larval-mortality test results?

options.A: A strong inverse correlation with coefficient −0.7853.
options.B: A strong positive correlation with coefficient +0.7853.

questions.rationale: Lower hatching was associated with greater mortality in the separate larval test, producing the reported negative correlation.
questions.evidence_quote: On comparing the two methods, we found a very good inverse correlation between the results obtained on effects of NPs on hatching rates and mortality test on the hatched larvae. The particles that reduced the hatching rate showed an increase in mortality in the ARC test using the normally hatched nauplii. The correlation test showed a coefficient of -0.7853.

questions.question: In the paired t-test comparing viability with hatching rates, what was the reported p-value and interpretation?

options.A: P=0.683, with no statistically significant difference in mean values.
options.C: P=0.05, exactly at the significance boundary.

questions.rationale: The paired comparison did not reveal a significant difference in mean values for the paired assay measures.
questions.evidence_quote: Comparing the viability of nauplii (inverse of mortality) in ARC test with the hatching rate showed no statistically significant difference in the mean values for each concentration of different particles (P=0.683) in the paired T test.

questions.question: Which nanoparticle behaved unusually at low concentration in the hatching experiment?

options.A: SiO2 at 10 mg/L had hatching and viability equivalent to controls.
options.B: Ag at 10 mg/L had hatching and viability equivalent to controls.
options.C: CuO at 10 mg/L improved hatching while eliminating viability.
options.D: ZnO at 10 mg/L caused complete hatching failure.

questions.rationale: The authors note that low-dose silica was not harmful by these outcomes and was comparable with the control.
questions.evidence_quote: SiO 2 nanoparticles at a concentration of 10mg/L displayed hatching rate and viability equivalent to the controls.

questions.question: What important exposure caveat did the authors observe in the standard larval test by 48 hours?

options.A: Nanoparticle sedimentation and flocculation occurred, potentially altering exposure.
options.B: All suspensions remained fully dispersed and chemically unchanged.
options.C: The larvae stopped feeding due to starvation at exactly 6 h.
options.D: The salt water pH shifted sharply above 10.

questions.rationale: The authors observed aggregation/sedimentation during the assay, which may change particle availability and complicate dose interpretation.
questions.evidence_quote: In the ARC test; we do see sedimentation and flocculation of nanoparticles by 48 hrs.

questions.question: How did the authors frame gut accumulation as a possible mechanism, and what alternative evidence suggested oxidative stress?

options.A: Gut clogging could contribute to death, while ROS/superoxide staining—especially for silver—suggested oxidative stress for some exposures.
options.B: Particles never entered the gut; mortality was exclusively due to starvation.
options.C: All nanoparticle mortality was proven to be oxidative and no gut uptake occurred.
options.D: Gut accumulation protected nauplii, and ROS staining occurred only in controls.

questions.rationale: The mechanism is proposed rather than conclusively proven: particles were seen in digestive tracts, and reactive oxygen staining was strongest for silver, with several other materials showing gut accumulation without staining.
questions.evidence_quote: The mortality observed may be due to the uptake of the eNPs clogging the gut as most of the nauplii in presence of eNPS show presence of particles in the digestive tract. In the hatching test, the dead Artemia and partially hatched cysts show increased stress in presence of nanoparticles as indicated by DCDFA staining. Even the nauplii exposed to some nanoparticles do show accumulation of ROS and superoxide especially with silver nanoparticles. But with remaining nanoparticles it must be the NP clogging in the gut that could cause mortality.
